title: Increasing Absolute Risk Aversion
prompt: Which property describes an investor who becomes less willing to take absolute risks as wealth increases?
solution:
Absolute risk aversion $A(w) = -u''(w)/u'(w)$ measures willingness to take risks of a fixed absolute size.
If the investor becomes less willing to take such risks as wealth grows, $A(w)$ rises with $w$: this is increasing absolute risk aversion (IARA). Quadratic utility is an example.
Under decreasing absolute risk aversion the investor would instead become more willing to take absolute risks as wealth increases.

subject: cm2
title: CAPM Assumptions
prompt: CAPM assumes:
options: Investors are risk-averse, choose portfolios on mean-variance criteria over a single period and have homogeneous expectations
solution:
CAPM adds assumptions to mean-variance portfolio theory: all investors are risk-averse and non-satiated, use the same one-period horizon, have homogeneous expectations, and can borrow and lend without limit at the risk-free rate in frictionless markets.
That every investor holds a combination of the market portfolio and the risk-free asset is a result of these assumptions, not an assumption itself.

solution: Intensity-based (reduced-form) models do not model the firm's assets. Default is a random event whose probability of occurring in a short interval $dt$ is approximately $\lambda(t)\,dt$. The intensity $\lambda(t)$ may be constant, time-dependent or itself stochastic.

subject: cm2
title: Hull-White Extension of Vasicek
prompt: Hull-White model extends Vasicek by:
options: Making the mean-reversion level time-dependent so the model fits the initial term structure
solution:
Hull-White: $dr_t = \alpha\left(\theta(t) - r_t\right)dt + \sigma\,dW_t$.
Replacing Vasicek's constant mean-reversion level with a deterministic function $\theta(t)$ lets the model reproduce the observed initial term structure of interest rates.

subject: cm2

title: Two-Asset Portfolio Variance

solution: Portfolio variance combines individual variances and the covariance term that captures how assets move together.

subject: cm2
title: Cox-Ingersoll-Ross Model Property
prompt: Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model ensures:
solution:
CIR: $dr_t = \alpha(\mu - r_t)\,dt + \sigma\sqrt{r_t}\,dW_t$.
The volatility $\sigma\sqrt{r_t}$ shrinks to zero as $r_t \to 0$, so the short rate cannot become negative. It stays strictly positive if $2\alpha\mu \ge \sigma^2$. Like Vasicek, the model is mean-reverting.

subject: cm2

solution: Reduced-form (intensity-based) models treat default as an exogenous stochastic event.

subject: cm2
title: Two-State Credit Model
prompt: A two-state credit model uses:
options: A transition intensity (hazard rate) from the non-default state to an absorbing default state
solution:
The two-state model has states N (not defaulted) and D (defaulted). Transitions from N to D occur with intensity $\lambda(t)$, and D is absorbing.
The probability of surviving to time $t$ is $\exp\left(-\int_0^t \lambda(s)\,ds\right)$. The intensity is often taken as constant, but it may depend on time.

subject: cm2
title: CAPM Expected Return Formula
prompt: Expected return in CAPM is calculated as:
options: Risk-free rate plus beta times market risk premium
solution: CAPM: $E[R_i] = r_f + \beta_i\left(E[R_M] - r_f\right)$, where $\beta_i = \operatorname{Cov}(R_i, R_M)/\operatorname{Var}(R_M)$.

subject: cm2

subject: cm2
title: Empirical Behaviour of Share Prices
prompt: Empirical evidence suggests stock prices:
options: Have log-returns that are more peaked with fatter tails than the normal distribution over short intervals
Have prices that are uncorrelated with their own past values
solution:
Empirical studies show the lognormal model fits poorly over short intervals. Daily or weekly log-returns are more peaked with fatter tails than a normal distribution (excess kurtosis), and volatility varies over time.
The lognormal approximation is better over longer intervals. Prices are strongly correlated with past prices; only returns are close to uncorrelated.

subject: cm2

subject: cm2
title: Lundberg Adjustment Coefficient
prompt: Lundberg’s adjustment coefficient is used to:
options: Give an upper bound for the infinite-time probability of ruin (Lundberg's inequality)
solution:
Lundberg's inequality: $\psi(u) \le e^{-Ru}$, where $R$ is the adjustment coefficient and $u$ the initial surplus.
A larger $R$ gives a tighter bound, so $R$ is used as a measure of the riskiness of the surplus process.

subject: cm2
title: Optimising Reinsurance via the Adjustment Coefficient
prompt: Maximizing the adjustment coefficient under reinsurance aims to:

subject: cm2
title: Inflation-Adjusted Chain Ladder
prompt: Run-off triangles can be adjusted for inflation by:
options: Restating past incremental claims in current money using an index of past inflation, then applying assumed future inflation to the projected payments
solution:
Inflation-adjusted chain ladder:
1. Restate each past incremental payment in current money using the observed (past) inflation index.
2. Accumulate and apply the chain ladder to project future incremental payments in current money.
3. Inflate each future payment to its payment date using assumed future inflation.
4. Sum the inflated future payments to obtain the reserve.

subject: cm2
title: Chain-Ladder Homogeneity Assumption
prompt: Chain ladder method assumes homogeneity in:
options: The development pattern across accident (origin) years
solution:
The basic chain ladder assumes every accident year develops in the same proportions, so the same development factors apply to all origin years.
This requires a homogeneous portfolio over time: a stable mix of business, claims handling and reporting patterns.

subject: cm2
title: Bornhuetter-Ferguson Emerging Claims
prompt: In the Bornhuetter-Ferguson method, the estimate of claims still to emerge for an accident year is based on:
options: The prior estimate of ultimate claims multiplied by the proportion still to develop
solution:
BF emerging claims $= \text{prior ultimate} \times \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{f}\right)$, where $f$ is the chain-ladder cumulative development factor to ultimate.
The prior ultimate is usually earned premium times an expected loss ratio. Estimated ultimate = claims to date + emerging claims.

subject: cm2
title: When to Use Average Cost per Claim
prompt: Average cost per claim method is most suitable when:
options: Reliable claim-number data are available, so claim numbers and average claim amounts can be projected separately
solution:
The average cost per claim method projects claim numbers and average claim amounts separately, each from its own triangle. It then multiplies projected ultimate claim numbers by projected ultimate average costs.
It needs reliable claim-number data and a consistent definition of a claim over time.

subject: cm2
title: Uncertainty in Reserve Projections

subject: cm2

solution: Monte Carlo simulation allows exploration of complex stochastic claims and reinsurance structures.

subject: cm2
title: Proportional Reinsurance and Ruin Probability
prompt: Effect of proportional reinsurance on finite-time ruin probability is to:
options: It may lower or raise it, depending on the reinsurance premium charged relative to the insurer's own premium loading
solution:
Ceding a proportion of each claim reduces the variability of retained claims, which tends to lower the probability of ruin.
But the insurer also pays a reinsurance premium. If the reinsurer's loading is higher than the insurer's, the insurer's retained loading falls and the probability of ruin can rise.
The overall effect therefore depends on the reinsurance terms.

subject: cm2

subject: cm2
title: Simulating Complex Reinsurance

subject: cm2
title: No-Arbitrage Bounds on a European Call
prompt: For a European call on a non-dividend-paying share, the no-arbitrage bounds on the call price $c$ are:
options: Lower bound $\max(0,\, S_0 - Ke^{-rT})$ and upper bound $S_0$
solution:
Upper bound: the call can never be worth more than the share, so $c \le S_0$.
Lower bound: a call plus cash $Ke^{-rT}$ is worth at least as much as the share at expiry, so $c \ge S_0 - Ke^{-rT}$. Also $c \ge 0$.
Hence $\max(0,\, S_0 - Ke^{-rT}) \le c \le S_0$.

subject: cm2
title: Value of a Forward Contract
prompt: At time $t$, what is the value of a long forward contract on a non-income-paying asset, with delivery price $K$ agreed earlier and delivery at time $T$?
solution:
Holding the long forward plus cash $Ke^{-r(T-t)}$ gives one unit of the asset at time $T$, so the forward is worth $S_t - Ke^{-r(T-t)}$, where $r$ is the continuously compounded risk-free rate.
This is zero at inception, when $K$ equals the forward price.

subject: cm2
title: Risk-Neutral Valuation Principle
prompt: Risk-neutral valuation prices a derivative by:
options: Taking the expected payoff under a risk-neutral measure and discounting at the risk-free rate
Assuming market returns follow CAPM exactly
solution:
Risk-neutral valuation does not assume investors are actually risk-neutral. A derivative that can be replicated has the same price whatever investors' risk preferences, so we may price it as if they were risk-neutral:
$$V_0 = e^{-rT}\,E_Q[\text{payoff}]$$

title: European Put Price Sensitivity
prompt: A European put option’s value increases when:
options: Expected dividends on the underlying decrease
solution:
A put pays $\max(K - S_T, 0)$, so a higher strike increases its value.
The put loses value when the share price rises, when volatility falls, and when expected dividends fall (lower dividends mean a higher expected share price). A fall in interest rates would increase a European put's value.

title: Option Vega Definition
prompt: Vega of an option measures:
options: Sensitivity of option price to volatility
Change in option price due to time
solution: Vega $= \partial V/\partial \sigma$, the sensitivity of the option price to volatility. It is often quoted per 1 percentage-point change in $\sigma$. Vega is positive for European calls and puts.

subject: cm2

solution: Rho $= \partial V/\partial r$, the sensitivity of the option price to the risk-free interest rate. It is often quoted per 1 percentage-point change in $r$. Rho is positive for European calls and negative for European puts.
